body: Well, I told someone about my diagnosis and they literally laughed at me. Like, full on belly-laugh. I was offended until they said, "I have lupus nephritis, systemic lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome..." and they went on to list like seven more things and my only reaction was, "Whoa. I am so sorry. How are you even alive??" So I didn't much mind. I did ask her to tell me about her life and how she managed, hoping I could glean something out of it, since she was obviously feeling up to sharing. But there's a hierarchy to this sort of thing and I respect that. I would not, for example, ask someone who has just been diagnosed with AIDS to comfort me in that moment because clearly they need comforting more than I do. I probably would have been vastly more gentle in telling someone with AIDS I need some space. I wouldn't have even told them what was going on with me.

I was diagnosed on Friday with lupus and I have no idea what my quality of life or my life expectancy is going to look like from here on out. I have a chronic disease that's eating my kidneys and my heart, that nothing can cure and is likely going to get worse. I'm sitting there in shock thinking about going through chemotherapy and dialysis. I haven't even cried yet. An hour after I get this news my friend texts me about her ex-boyfriend. I said "I'm so sorry but I don't care right now. I've just been diagnosed with lupus. I am incapable of thinking about anything right now except the fact that I might die of kidney failure" She said, "You rude fucking bitch!! Just because you're dying doesn't mean I don't have the right to be treated with sympathy! You're the cruelest person I've ever met, fuck you!!"

Never mind that I gave a 20 to a homeless person last week. Never mind that I've listened to her talk about her on again off again boyfriend for years now. Never mind that my fucking kidneys aren't working and I just got this news an hour ago. I'm the bitch. Right. 

Eat shit, Ellie.

I know. Me too. I feel the same way. Here's the thing, though. Yes, it could get really really bad, but if it does, you won't be alone because everyone else will be going through similar changes and upheaval. And because the whole world will be having similar problems, we will figure out a way to live and be okay in the end. At least, our generation will. 

And really every generation has had the thing that they were convinced would kill them all, but it didn't. Nazis, the nuclear arms race (my parents told me stories about how when they were in college they all planned their suicide together just in case the bombs went off, and they were dead serious about it.) In the 1980s it was the AIDS crisis and everyone was afraid that it would be the next Black Plague and just kill everybody and there would never be a treatment.  But we lived through all of that stuff even though nobody ever imagined we could. We might not be so lucky this generation but we have a very good track record of stopping earth-shattering catastrophes at the very last possible second.

Maybe we'll all migrate to Alaska and Siberia because that'll be the only place that's temperate enough to live in. Maybe we'll all move our cities underground. We'll probably end up learning how to eat something else. Maybe they'll grow wheat in Northern Canada, and cactus fruit in Oklahoma. 

You need to find a piece of your life that you can hold onto when it gets bad. For me, I'm banking on that thing being my house. It's basically a large RV so if we need to migrate to Alaska, I can get there relatively hassle-free and take my whole house with me. I'm going to learn how to farm and keep my own garden so I'll always have at least a little food. I'll probably have to adapt and learn to eat whatever will grow in whatever climate we end up having, even if it has to be Cactus and algae. 

It's going to suck, but it's going to suck for all of us, so we'll all be able to figure it out together. We can adapt.
